It is widely used in the Andean regions of Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, northern Chile and north-western Argentina, and exists in many variant forms. At gatherings of folk musicians after the Chilean coup it was banned along with the quena, which shows that it belongs to the context of Andean folk performance.

查蘭戈琴是安地斯高原的小型撥弦魯特琴，霍恩博斯泰爾—薩克斯分類編號321.321: The charango is a small plucked lute of the Andean highlands, Hornbostel–Sachs classification 321.321-5, which comes from the Quechua and Aymara peoples. It is about 66 cm long, traditionally with an armadillo shell as its soundbox and now mostly wooden, with a gourd also used for children's instruments. It usually has ten strings in five courses of two, and variants with four to fifteen strings also exist. It is used mainly for traditional Andean music and is popular in Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, northern Chile and north-western Argentina; its players are called charanguistas.
查蘭戈琴為安地斯小型魯特琴類撥弦樂器，於殖民後由西班牙人帶來維烏埃拉琴等弦樂器後: The charango is a small Andean plucked lute. It developed after the conquest, once the Spanish had brought string instruments such as the vihuela; its direct origin is uncertain, and it may be connected with the vihuela, the bandurria or the lute. One account has it taking shape in Potosí around the beginning of the eighteenth century, supported by a church carving of 1744. It spread through Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, northern Chile and north-western Argentina; a document of 1814 already records its use, and after the Chilean coup of 1973 it was banned along with the quena.
